findings: Frontal chest radiograph obtained with patient supine or semi-erect, EKG monitoring leads overlying the neck and upper chest
Cardiomediastinal silhouette is midline; heart size appears within upper limits of normal given projection

Bilateral lung fields are grossly aerated; there is increased opacity/haziness in the perihilar and lower zones bilaterally, more pronounced on the right, which may reflect atelectasis, effusion, or technique-related rotation

A well-defined horizontal air-fluid level is seen in the left lower hemithorax, suggestive of either a large hiatal hernia with air-fluid level or a hydropneumothorax; correlation with lateral view and clinical history is recommended
Visualized osseous structures (ribs, spine) appear intact without obvious fracture
No definite free air under the diaphragm is clearly identified on this single view
Soft tissue overlying the shoulders and chest wall appears symmetric

Further evaluation with lateral chest X-ray, CT, or clinical correlation (e.g., recent surgery, chest tube placement, trauma) is advised to differentiate.

summary: This chest X-ray shows the lungs, heart, and surrounding bones. There is a notable finding on the left lower side of the chest: a horizontal line where air sits above fluid, called an 'air-fluid level.' This is most commonly seen when part of the stomach has slipped up into the chest (a hiatal hernia) and contains both air and fluid, which is a fairly common and often benign condition. However, in some cases a similar appearance can be caused by a mixture of air and fluid within the space around the lung (called a hydropneumothorax), which can be more serious, especially after surgery, injury, or infection. There is also some cloudiness at the bottom of both lungs, which could be from mild lung collapse (atelectasis), fluid buildup, or simply the angle of the X-ray. Because a single X-ray view can't fully tell these possibilities apart, doctors typically recommend a side view (lateral X-ray), a CT scan, or looking at the patient's symptoms and history (such as recent surgery, chest tube, or trauma) to determine the exact cause. This report is a preliminary AI-generated observation and must be confirmed by a qualified radiologist.
